one_liner: Hash-counting Rust replacement for 'sort | uniq -c | sort -n'; 5.3x faster than the LC_ALL=C pipeline (first-party).
what_it_does: hist reads lines from a file or stdin, counts each distinct line and prints 'count<TAB>line' sorted by count (ascending by default; -d descending, -n by line, -S unsorted), with -m/-M count filters, -k to keep the top k plus an 'other lines' summary, and regex include (-i), exclude (-e) and substitution (-s) applied before counting. With -u it instead streams each line's first occurrence in input order, like awk '!seen[$0]++'. It is a standalone binary, not a library, and its output format is not the same as uniq -c.
how_it_is_fast: Every line goes through one hashbrown HashMap<&[u8], usize> lookup via the raw-entry API; a new line is copied once into a bumpalo arena, and only the distinct entries are sorted, by an integer count with sort_unstable. The pipeline it replaces sorts every input line (n log n string comparisons, locale collation by default), pipes them through uniq and sorts again, across three processes. Lines are read as raw bytes with bstr's for_byte_line, so there is no UTF-8 validation on input. The gain is algorithmic (hash aggregation instead of sort-based grouping), not a language effect.
when_to_use: Histogram of repeated values (log fields, tokens, k-mers, FASTQ headers or sequences) where the distinct set fits comfortably in RAM.
Replacing 'sort | uniq -c | sort -n' in shell pipelines when you only need counts ordered by abundance, not the stable tie order of sort.
Count with filtering or normalisation in one pass (regex include, exclude or substitution before counting) instead of chaining grep and sed.
Order-preserving dedup of a stream (-u) of plain-text lines that contain no commas, double quotes or carriage returns.
when_not_to_use: Inputs whose distinct lines may not fit in memory: everything goes into an in-memory arena and hash table with no spill to disk, while sort does an external merge and -S bounds its memory.

Pipelines that parse uniq -c output: hist prints count<TAB>line through a CSV writer, so lines containing a tab, double quote or CR are quoted, and ties come out in hash order that can change between runs.
Data that may not be valid UTF-8 (Latin-1 logs, binary records): writing a non-UTF-8 line returns an error and aborts the run.
Very large single files on many cores: hist is single-threaded (multi-threading is open issue #16 and PR #17), while GNU sort uses several threads by default and cuniq has --threads and --memmap.
CSV or FASTQ dedup with -u: see the quoting gotcha below.

integration.form: binary (crate hist-rs on crates.io, binary name hist)
integration.dependencies: hashbrown 0.16, bumpalo 3, bstr 1, csv 1.4, regex 1.12, clap 4.5, anyhow
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.88+ in practice (edition 2024 and let-chains in main.rs; no rust-version declared on crates.io)
integration.platforms: any platform Rust supports; no platform-specific code
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same counts as sort | uniq -c | sort -n, but a different output format (count<TAB>line, CSV quoting), unstable tie order, CR LF folded into LF and errors on non-UTF-8 lines

gotchas: Dedup mode quotes data: 'hist -u' writes each first-seen line through csv::Writer with the default ',' delimiter, so any line containing a comma, double quote, CR or LF is wrapped in double quotes with inner quotes doubled, and an empty line becomes "". Deduplicating a CSV file or real FASTQ (Phred+33 quality strings include ',' and '"') therefore changes the data. The benchmark input (nucgen headers, ACGT sequences, '+' and '?' quality strings) contains none of these bytes, so the published numbers are unaffected.

Counting mode uses a tab-delimited CSV writer, so lines containing a tab or double quote are quoted; lines ending in CR LF and in LF are counted as the same line because bstr's for_byte_line strips both terminators.

The headline 24.35x compares against sort in the default locale (export LC_ALL= then sort | uniq -c | sort -n); the final sort -n then orders about 2M count-1 ties by full-line locale collation, work hist does not do. With LC_ALL=C the gap is 5.27x, against single-threaded uutils sort 3.84x, and an independent run in issue #3 (pixelb, Linux GNU sort, LC_ALL=C, 10M FASTQ records) measured 12.864 s vs 36.238 s, about 2.8x (derived from page data).

The repo's .cargo/config.toml adds -C target-cpu=native, but cargo install ignores project-level config, so 'cargo install hist-rs' as the README instructs produces a generic build; the README does not say which build was benchmarked.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick hist over huniq (12.16x slower on this workload) and cuniq (2.43x slower) for single-threaded in-memory counting sorted by abundance with regex prefiltering; pick cuniq for multi-gigabyte files where its --memmap and --threads modes matter, and runiq when dedup must run in bounded memory.
verified_claims_summary: First-party hyperfine runs (10 warmups) on a MacBook M3 Pro over a 1M-record FASTQ (4M lines, about 2M distinct) from nucgen: hist 231.5 ms vs default-locale 'sort | uniq -c | sort -n' 5637.6 ms (24.35x), LC_ALL=C 1219.5 ms (5.27x), uutils sort --parallel 1 890.1 ms (3.84x) and awk 1265.4 ms (5.47x); dedup mode 180.6 ms vs awk '!seen[$0]++' 1307.1 ms (7.24x). The sort, uniq and awk binaries' implementations and versions are not stated, and an independent Linux run in issue #3 puts the like-for-like (LC_ALL=C) gap near 2.8x.
status_note: Active through December 2025 (54 commits, 120 stars, hist-rs 0.1.8 on crates.io with 1,318 downloads, an open multi-threading PR #17); MIT is declared in Cargo.toml but the repo has no LICENSE file (the README badge links a missing LICENSE.md); fine as a CLI for in-memory counting, but -u mangles lines containing commas or quotes.
